newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Public Bank plans foreign holding change.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Public Bank plans foreign holding change.

text.p: Malaysia's Public Bank Bhd said this week it planned to change its shareholding rules, a move that analysts interpret as allowing foreigners to hold more than the current 30 percent limit.
The amendment would allow foreigners to hold shares previously allocated only for Malaysians.
The catch was that foreign shareholders would no longer have voting rights, although they would be entitled to dividends and other benefits, analysts said.

"The directors have resolved to grant all rights, benefits, powers and privileges, except for voting rights, to those restricted shares... of foreigners and which exceed the maximum 30 percent limit," said Public Bank.
The bank also said: "The rationale for withholding voting rights of such restricted shares is in order to limit control (which is exercised through the right to vote) by foreigners."
The statement caused a run on the share price of the foreign tranche which fell 50 cents to 3.92 ringgit in late trading on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, arbitraging activity lifted local shares to gain 24 cents to 3.56 ringgit, analysts said.
Both shares were heavily traded, with Public Bank's foreign shares topping the most-active list with 22 million shares traded.

"Dealers are arbitraging the two stocks. I would switch over to the local shares, since the foreign tranche is trading at a premium," said Franklin Tan, vice president of research at Y.K. Fung Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
Tan said local shares in Public Bank owned by foreigners who wanted to register themselves as formal shareholders would immediately be converted to "foreign" shares without voting rights.

"The current ruling does not allow foreign shareholders to own more than 30 percent of the bank. The amendment would allow foreigners to buy into the local shares, but without having the voting rights," said Audrey Ho, head of research at Mohaiyani Securities.
"Theoretically there is no limit to foreign shareholding any more," Ho said.
Public Bank said approvals had already been received from Malaysia's central Bank Negara and the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange for the move.
Shareholders would vote on the proposal in the extraordinary general meeting due to be held on June 17 in Kuala Lumpur.
Public Bank officials could not immediately be reached for comment.
